mc-01.title: Models of Communication
explain: All day long we speak, write, read, and watch. When someone conveys thoughts or information to another person and receives them in turn, we call this **communication**. Media communication examines what happens when this process passes through media such as newspapers, broadcasting, and the internet. The media and articles in this course are all fictional, invented to aid understanding, and have no connection to any real news organization or platform.

The most basic explanatory framework consists of five elements.
- **Sender**: the party who creates and sends the message.
- **Message**: the content to be conveyed. It can be speech, writing, images, or sound.
- **Medium**: the channel that carries the message. Examples include paper, radio waves, screens, and face-to-face conversation.
- **Receiver**: the party who receives and interprets the message.
- **Noise**: any interference that blurs or alters the message.

explain.alt: From the left, boxes for sender, medium, and receiver are connected by arrows, with the word message above the arrows. An orange noise box sits above the medium box, and a line looping back, labeled feedback, runs below.
explain.caption: The basic communication model

explain: Noise is not limited to loud sound. Text that is too small, unfamiliar technical terms, and a receiver who is distracted by something else are all noise. When the meaning the sender intended differs from the meaning the receiver understood, this is mostly explained as a sign that noise crept in somewhere.

Early models drew the message as flowing in one direction only. Real conversation, however, goes back and forth: the receiver nods or asks a question, and the sender adjusts what they say accordingly. The receiver's response returning to the sender is called **feedback**. In media with very many receivers, such as broadcasting or newspapers, feedback is slow and weak, so it is hard for the sender to know the response.

examples.title: A fictional village announcement
body: The village head of Gana Village announced over the village loudspeaker, "We will clean the stream tomorrow at 9 a.m." But a tractor happened to be loud during the broadcast, and one resident heard "9" as "5."

The sender is the village head, the message is the cleanup notice, the medium is the village loudspeaker, and the receiver is the resident. The tractor sound is noise. If the resident later phones to ask, "What time did you say?", that is feedback.

mc-02.title: The Changing Media
explain: The ways people exchange information have changed greatly over time. Simplified a great deal, they can be divided into five stages. Because stages overlapped in real history and the pace differed by region, this is a broad division meant to aid understanding.

- **Oral era**: relies on speech and memory. Stories are passed on through song and recitation and vanish the moment they are spoken.
- **Writing era**: records in written characters, preserving information across time and distance. However, copying by hand required much labor, so the number of readers was limited.
- **Print era**: the same text can be produced in large numbers, so books and newspapers spread. Many people receive the same message at the same time.
- **Electronic era**: the era of radio and television, which send sound and images instantly over long distances by radio waves. They can be received even by people who cannot read.
- **Digital era**: information is converted into numbers, so copying, storing, and transmitting become nearly free, and ordinary people too can become senders.

One view holds that when the medium changes, it is not only the message that changes but also how people gather and think. For example, print is explained as having increased the habit of reading quietly alone, and electronic media as having increased the experience of watching the same scene at the same time. However, there are objections to asserting that media determine society, because the needs of society also shape how media are used.

One of the biggest changes of the digital era is that the **boundary between sender and receiver** has blurred. Where once a few institutions sent and the many received, now anyone can post text and video and respond immediately to others' posts. This widened opportunities for voice, but there is also the assessment that the volume of information has become overwhelming and the burden of judging what is trustworthy has shifted to the receiver.

examples.title: The same news, different routes
body: A new bridge opened in the fictional country of Ganara. In the oral era, the news would have spread slowly by word of mouth at the marketplace. In the print era, the next day's newspaper delivered the same article to many homes. In the electronic era, that evening's broadcast showed the opening ceremony. In the digital era, a citizen who crossed the bridge can post photos and impressions on the spot.
Each time the route changes, the speed, the reach, and the senders of the news change.

mc-03.title: Making the News
explain: Countless things happen in the world every day. Only a tiny fraction of them become **news**. News is not a mirror of events exactly as they happened; it is a product that someone has selected and shaped. Understanding this process does not mean doubting the news; it means reading the news with knowledge of how it is made.

The criteria that decide what becomes news are commonly called **news values**. They are organized differently by country and by outlet, but the ones frequently cited are as follows.
- **Timeliness**: how recent the event is.
- **Impact**: how many people it affects.
- **Proximity**: whether it is close to the reader, geographically or psychologically.
- **Prominence**: whether well-known people or institutions are involved.
- **Conflict**: whether opinions or interests clash.
- **Unusualness**: whether it is out of the ordinary.

Even events with high news value are not all published, because print space and broadcast time are limited. Reporters and editors choose what to cover and decide the length and placement of articles. The person or stage that decides which items to let through and which to filter out is called a **gatekeeper**, and the process is called **gatekeeping**.

explain.alt: A funnel of four boxes connected by arrows from top to bottom. The boxes narrow progressively in this order: all events that happened, selection of what to cover, editing and placement decisions, and publication.
explain.caption: The gatekeeping funnel

explain: Gatekeeping is not a bad thing. Since not everything can fit in limited space, selection is unavoidable. The problem arises when the selection criteria are invisible. The reason the same event on the same day receives different weight in different outlets is explained as being that their selection criteria differ slightly.

examples.title: A fictional editorial meeting
body: Three items came up at the editorial meeting of the Gana Daily today: (1) a main downtown road will be closed all day, (2) a big event will be held in a distant country, and (3) a hundred-year-old resident of a village has just learned to ride a bicycle.

Item 1 affects the day of many readers, so its impact and proximity are high. Item 2 is large in scale but far from readers. Item 3 is rare, so it has unusualness. Because space is limited, the editor-in-chief decided to put item 1 first and run item 3 briefly. Another editor-in-chief might decide differently.

mc-04.title: Framing and Agenda-Setting
explain: If the news does not reflect reality exactly as it is, how does the news affect what people think? Media research often uses two concepts to explain this.

The first is **agenda-setting**. This is the idea that when the media cover a story often and prominently, people tend to regard it as an important problem. It is often expressed as the media influencing "what to think about." To what extent, and under what conditions, this holds differs from study to study.

The second is **framing**. This is the idea that even the same facts are received differently depending on which aspects are put first and which words are used to name them. It is similar to how what you see changes depending on how a photo is cropped. A frame is different from a lie. The facts themselves are the same; the emphasis and wording differ.

explain.alt: A common facts box sits at the top. The lower left card is titled Gana City library operations made more efficient, and the lower right card is titled Gana City library opening hours reduced. Arrows run from the common facts box to the two cards.
explain.caption: The same facts, different headlines

explain: The purpose of understanding framing is not to judge one side as bad. Every text chooses certain words and an order, so no text is entirely free of frames. What matters is to (1) notice that a frame exists, (2) separate out what the common facts are, and (3) ask whether any information is missing.

When comparing several headlines, check the following.
1. What is the **fact** that the headlines have in common?
2. Which words carry evaluation or emotion?
3. What information is absent from the headline but present in the body text?

examples.title: Two fictional headlines
body: Suppose Gana City has decided to cut the weekday opening hours of the city library by 2 hours (fictional). One newspaper wrote "Gana City makes library operations more efficient," and another wrote "Gana City reduces library opening hours."

Both headlines share the fact that the opening hours were cut. The first headline focuses on a change in how the library is run, and the second on the reduction in time available to users. This example does not say which is right. What the reader should do is check how the body text describes the reason for the cut, the hours cut, and the effect on users.

mc-05.title: The Information Environment
explain: In the past, the channels for obtaining information were limited to one or two newspapers or a few broadcasters. Today, internet services often decide **what to show first** from among countless texts and videos. Let us call the composition of the information a person encounters each day the **information environment**. This lesson is a general explanation that assumes fictional services and does not describe how any real service works.

A **recommendation algorithm** is a method by which a computer, following set rules, chooses texts or videos to show a user. In general, it selects similar items based on records such as what the user read and watched for a long time, and what they reacted to. As a result, it has the advantage of making it easy to find things of interest.

explain.alt: A cycle diagram of four boxes connected by arrows in a clockwise direction. The order is: reads an article, reading record accumulates, similar articles recommended, reads more. The word feedback is written in the center.
explain.caption: The feedback loop of recommendation

explain: However, there is a concern that when this cycle repeats, similar articles keep appearing and the range of what one encounters may narrow. This is commonly called a **filter bubble**, but how much it actually appears and how large it is vary by study, and there is debate. It also varies with how much users themselves seek out diverse sources.

A similar but separate concept is **confirmation bias**. This is not a service but a mental habit of people. People are explained as tending to accept information that fits what they already think, and to brush off or doubt information that does not. If recommendation increases similar articles and confirmation bias makes people accept them more readily, the two forces can reinforce each other.

That does not mean recommendation should be seen only as bad. What matters is knowing that one's screen has been selected, and having the habit of sometimes searching for and comparing things directly.

examples.title: A day on a fictional video service
body: Dara watched a few cooking videos on a fictional video service. The next day the recommendation list had more cooking videos, and Dara watched those too. A few days later, half of the home screen is cooking videos.

Since Dara was interested in cooking, this may be convenient. However, if Dara was also interested in local news, that news may have been pushed off the screen. If Dara searches for local news directly, the screen changes again.

mc-06.title: Source-Checking Procedure
explain: Let us connect the earlier lessons. News is selected, passes through frames, and reaches me through recommendation. That is why we need the habit of checking the **source** before believing or spreading the text in front of us. The source refers to where and through whom the information came.

It helps to have a set order for checking. One example follows. This is only a suggestion, and steps can be added or removed depending on the situation.
1. **Summarize the claim**: write the text's core claim in one sentence.
2. **Check the publisher**: look at who published it, who wrote it, and for what purpose.
3. **Find the original material**: locate the original place of the data or statement the text cites as evidence.
4. **Cross-check with other sources**: see whether other, independent sources say the same thing.
5. **Decide whether to share**: believe and pass on only as much as has been verified. If it has not been verified, say so or do not pass it on.

An **independent source** means a source that confirmed the matter separately without copying from others. Ten outlets that copied the same text count as one. Also look at the publication date, because old articles sometimes circulate as though they were current.

Finally, checking does not always split things neatly into true and false. In some cases part is true but context is missing, and in some cases it cannot yet be verified. In such cases, think in terms of "the verified part" and "the unverified part."

examples.title: Two fictional articles
body: Suppose there is news that a public swimming pool in the fictional Nana City is raising its admission fee. The two articles below were invented for this exercise.

**Article A** (Nana Daily, March 2) "Nana City raises pool fee by 1,000 won. The city said that "facility maintenance costs have increased" and that it will apply from April. According to the city's public notice, the adult fee goes from 4,000 won to 5,000 won."
**Article B** (Nana News, no date shown) "Nana City pool fee bombshell! Citizens furious. People are saying ordinary folks can no longer even swim. One citizen said, "Everyone is angry.""

Article A gives the date, the publisher, and the original material, the city's public notice, and states specific amounts. Article B has no date, no supporting material, and many generalizations and emotional expressions such as "Everyone is angry." However, this alone does not let us conclude that Article B is false. We can only say there is not enough evidence to check.

mc-07.title: Agenda-Setting and Priming: Does Coverage Volume Transfer Importance?
explain: During election season, people name a few similar issues as "the most important problems right now." Where does that list come from? It might be built up from what each person experiences in daily life, or it might be shaped by the issues that newspapers and broadcasters put first every day. **Agenda-setting** is the theory that formally asks about the latter possibility.

McCombs and Shaw surveyed undecided voters in a small town during the 1968 US presidential election. The ranking of issues that voters named as important was very similar to the ranking of issues that the local media covered prominently. When this result was published in 1972, the name agenda-setting took hold. The core claim is that the media influence the list of **what people think is important** rather than directly changing people's **opinions**.

Let us sort out the terms. When the media transfer the salience (degree of prominence) of an **object**, namely an issue, to citizens, this is **first-level agenda-setting**. When the salience of the **attributes** that describe the same object (for example, whether a candidate's competence or morality) also transfers, it is called **second-level agenda-setting**, which borders on framing. **Priming**, meanwhile, is the effect whereby an issue that the news has made prominent becomes activated in people's memory and is used as the **yardstick for evaluating** politicians or policies. Iyengar and Kinder applied this concept to research on political news.

explain.alt: A bar chart by issue for a fictional city. For each issue, a gray bar (share of January newspaper coverage) is paired with a green bar (share of March citizen responses). Transportation: gray 45, green 36. Housing: gray 25, green 30. Environment: gray 20, green 24. Culture: gray 10, green 10. The bars of each color sum to 100%.
explain.caption: Share of coverage and share of citizen responses

explain: The figure uses data from a fictional city. The larger an issue's share of newspaper coverage in January, the larger its share in citizen responses in March. The ranking is the same: transportation, housing, environment, culture. But looking at the numbers, for transportation the coverage share (45) is higher than the response share (36), while for housing it is the reverse (25 versus 30). This means citizens' sense of importance does not simply copy the volume of coverage. The fact that the rankings match alone does not allow us to conclude that **coverage moved citizens**. The newspaper may have followed citizens' interests, or both may have responded to real events.

That is why design matters in agenda-setting research. First, secure the **time order**. If coverage volume is measured first and citizen responses are measured after a time lag, the possibility that citizens led the coverage can be partly ruled out. Next, control for **third factors** such as the actual size of the issue itself (for example, the number of accidents) or personal experience. The clearest evidence comes from experiments. Participants are shown different news compositions, and researchers see whether importance responses move accordingly.

The limits are also clear. It is discussed that for issues citizens experience directly in daily life, such as unemployment or housing prices, reliance on the media is lower and the effect may be weaker. Conversely, for diplomacy or events in distant regions that cannot be experienced directly, dependence on the media grows. The size of the effect also varies with the audience's interest, political knowledge, and conversation partners. Agenda-setting should be read not as "the media decide everything" but as a conditional theory that "under certain conditions it influences the ranking of importance."

examples.title: Reading the differences in the figure
body: Given: for each issue in the figure's data, subtract the coverage share from the citizen response share.
Step 1: Transportation 36 − 45 = −9, housing 30 − 25 = +5, environment 24 − 20 = +4, culture 10 − 10 = 0.

Step 2: The issue with the largest absolute difference is transportation (9 percentage points). Interpretation: Even though the rankings are the same, citizen responses did not simply follow the volume of coverage. Citizens saw housing and environment as more important than the coverage did, and transportation as less important. This suggests there are factors other than coverage volume, such as life experience.

examples.title: Reading a priming case (fictional)
body: Given: In the fictional city of Haneul City, news about flood damage was reported daily for three weeks. Before the coverage, the correlation between evaluation of the mayor and satisfaction with disaster-prevention policy was 0.30, and after the coverage it was 0.55.

Step 1: The flood coverage activated the issue of disaster prevention in memory. Step 2: When citizens evaluated the mayor, disaster-prevention policy was used as a yardstick with greater weight. The correlation rising from 0.30 to 0.55 is the trace of that.

Interpretation: This is priming. Rather than opinions about the mayor themselves being changed by the news, the weight of the criteria used in evaluation changed. However, since the cause cannot be established from the change in correlation alone, other events during the same period must also be checked.

mc-08.title: Framing Effects: Same Facts, Different Frames
explain: "Factory closure leaves 400 people without jobs" and "Even with the factory closure, 200 people keep their jobs" can state the same fact (when the total is 600). Yet readers react differently. The first sentence evokes loss, the second preservation. The phenomenon in which the frame in which the same reality is described changes interpretation and judgment is called the **framing effect**.

Entman summarized framing as **selecting** part of reality and making it more **salient**, and divided what frames do into four functions. They **define** what the problem is, interpret its **cause**, make a **moral evaluation** of the object, and suggest a **remedy**. When the same event is framed as a "crime problem," the cause tends to be an individual's deviance and the remedy punishment; when framed as a "social problem," the cause tends to be structure and the remedy institutional improvement.

Frame research broadly distinguishes two kinds. **Emphasis framing** highlights different aspects of the same issue (economics, safety, fairness, and so on), while **equivalence framing** rewords logically identical information in terms of gains ("200 saved") or losses ("400 lost"). Iyengar also divided news into the **episodic frame**, centered on the stories of individual people, and the **thematic frame**, centered on statistics and institutional context, and held that the former tends to attribute responsibility to individuals.

Let us look at equivalence framing with numbers. In a fictional situation where 600 jobs are at risk, the two options in the gain frame are "A: 200 jobs are saved for certain" and "B: with probability 1/3 all 600 jobs are saved, and with probability 2/3 none are saved." The expected value of B is 1/3 × 600 = 200, the same as A. The two options in the loss frame are "C: 400 jobs are lost for certain" and "D: with probability 1/3 nothing is lost, and with probability 2/3 all 600 are lost." The expected loss of D is 2/3 × 600 = 400, the same as C. The four options have the same expected value and differ only in wording. This is the structure of the classic experiment shown by Kahneman and Tversky. They reported a tendency to choose the certain option more often in the gain frame and the gambling option more often in the loss frame.

The paths through which a frame has its effect are explained by **accessibility** and **applicability**. The effect is larger to the extent that a frame makes certain thoughts easy to bring to mind (accessibility) and makes people feel those thoughts fit the present judgment (applicability). Therefore the size of a framing effect is related not only to the strength of the frame but also to the thoughts the audience already holds.

Let us note the limits. In real news environments, different frames compete. There is research showing that when people are exposed to competing frames together, the effect of one frame is reduced or the frames cancel each other out. Also, people with strong beliefs or those familiar with the issue are less swayed by frames. The existence of a frame is itself a neutral analytic tool, and which frame is right must be judged separately on the evidence. Since all reporting involves selection, there is no reporting without a frame.

examples.title: Breaking down a frame by its four functions
body: Given: A fictional article, "Local Garbage Crisis," states, "Illegal dumping by some residents is the cause, and stricter enforcement is the solution."

Step 1: The problem definition is illegal dumping, the causal interpretation is the behavior of some residents, the moral evaluation is blame for those who broke the rules, and the remedy is stricter enforcement.

Step 2: If the same event is reported as "the collection system failed to keep up with population growth," the cause becomes the system and the remedy becomes expanded collection. Interpretation: It is not that the facts differ, but that the selected aspect differs, so all four functions change.

examples.title: Checking equivalence by expected value
body: Given: A fictional notice says, "The new program saves 600 of the 1,200 participants," and "Even with the new program, 600 cannot be saved."

Step 1: The 600 saved in the first sentence plus the 600 not saved in the second sum to 1,200, so the two sentences state the same fact. Step 2: Because it is logically the same information, this case is equivalence framing.

Interpretation: If people who read the two sentences evaluate them differently, that difference is an effect of wording, not a difference in information. What the reader should do is check the denominator and the total directly, whichever wording is used.

checks.explanation: The four functions are problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and remedy suggestion.

Says who or what produced that problem

checks.explanation: 2/3 × 600 = 400. So it has the same expected value as option C, which loses 400 jobs for certain.

checks.explanation: The episodic frame is held to tend to produce interpretations of individual responsibility, but this does not mean it does so for every reader. There is no reporting without a frame.

mc-09.title: Cultivation Theory and the Spiral of Silence: Accumulating Perceptions and Watchful Opinions
explain: Do people who have watched a lot of television for a long time feel the world is more dangerous? And when I feel my opinion differs from the majority's, do I become hesitant to speak? If the previous two lessons dealt with the cognition created by a single exposure, this lesson deals with **effects that accumulate over a long time** and the **social psychology through which public opinion forms**.

Gerbner's **cultivation theory** holds that the media do not deliver a particular message briefly but provide a **system of repeated stories and images** over a long period, and that the more people watch, the more their perception of reality comes to resemble that media world. Consider a fictional survey. If the share agreeing with "The world is a dangerous place" is 62% among **heavy viewers**, who watch 4 or more hours a day, and 44% among **light viewers**, who watch 1 hour or less a day, then the 18-percentage-point difference is the **cultivation differential**. Gerbner called this perception of reality the "mean world syndrome" and linked it to broadcasting with a lot of violence.

Two concepts accompany cultivation theory. **Mainstreaming** is the convergence of perceptions of groups with different dispositions toward a single point the more they watch, and **resonance** is the effect becoming larger when what is watched overlaps with the viewer's actual experience. Many limitations are also pointed out. It is common for the differential to shrink greatly once **other factors** such as age, gender, and area of residence are controlled, and the **reverse direction** is also possible: anxious people may watch more broadcasts.

Noelle-Neumann's **spiral of silence** starts from the premise that people, as social beings, have a **fear of isolation**. People look around and gauge which opinion is dominant using a **quasi-statistical sense**. If they believe their opinion is that of the majority, they speak publicly; if they believe it is that of a minority, they stay silent. The side with more people speaking sounds louder and the silent side looks smaller, so this gap grows like a spiral. Here the media serve as a window that tells people what the dominant opinion is.

Let us follow the progression of the spiral with numbers. At first, those publicly expressing opinion are 60 people with opinion A and 40 with opinion B. In round 1, if 1/4 of the B expressers fall silent, B becomes 40 × 3/4 = 30 people. In round 2, if 1/3 of the remaining B fall silent again, B becomes 30 × 2/3 = 20 people. A remains at 60, so A's share among public expressers rises from the initial 60% to 60/80 = 75%. Even if the actual distribution of opinion does not change, the **heard distribution** changes.

This theory too comes with conditions. A **hard core** group, whose members hold their beliefs so strongly that they are unaffected by pressure from the majority, does not fall silent. In communities where a minority sharing the same opinion gathers, or in anonymous spaces, minority opinion can be voiced and the spiral can weaken. It is discussed that the stronger the moral coloring of the issue, the stronger the spiral, but the evidence varies by study. Both cultivation theory and the spiral of silence should be read not as theories in which the media one-sidedly move individuals, but as hypotheses explaining how repeated exposure and the social environment shape perception.

examples.title: Calculating the cultivation differential
body: Given: In a fictional survey, the share agreeing that "Night streets are dangerous" is 62% among heavy viewers and 44% among light viewers. After controlling for age and area of residence, it becomes 54% for heavy viewers and 48% for light viewers.
Step 1: The cultivation differential before control is 62 − 44 = 18 percentage points. Step 2: After control, the differential shrank to 54 − 48 = 6 percentage points.

Interpretation: Two thirds of the difference was explained by other factors such as age and region, and 6 percentage points remain. Whether the remaining difference is a cultivation effect or reverse direction cannot be known from this data alone. For this reason, cultivation research is required to use controls and time-lagged designs.

examples.title: Calculating the progression of the spiral
body: Given: In a fictional debate, those publicly expressing opinion are 80 in favor and 20 opposed. In each round, half of the expressers on the minority side fall silent.
Step 1: After round 1, the opposed are 20 × 1/2 = 10. Step 2: After round 2, the opposed are 5. The in-favor remain at 80, so their share is 80/85, about 94%.

Interpretation: The in-favor side was already ahead at 80% at the start, but after only two rounds it appears to rise to 94%. This theory predicts that it is the distribution of public expression, not the actual distribution of opinion, that becomes biased. Whether the 5 who fell silent are privately opposed cannot be confirmed from expression data.

mc-10.title: Gatekeeping and News Values: What Becomes News
explain: Countless events happen in a day, but only a few appear on a news front page. Who chooses, and by what criteria? Answering this question is the starting point of **journalism studies**. The process of selection is called **gatekeeping**, and the criteria of selection are called **news values**.

Gatekeeping is a term Lewin used while analyzing the paths by which food enters the household; it is a model in which someone decides whether information passes as it goes through a gate. White applied the concept to news by observing the wire-news editor of a local newspaper. The point that news selection is made not by one editor's taste but through multiple layers of gates led to later research.

As criteria for selection, the **news factors** summarized by Galtung and Ruge in 1965 are the classic. Later studies refined them, and timeliness, proximity, scale of impact, conflict, prominence, and unusualness are named as news values. As in the figure of this lesson, scoring each event on each factor becomes a tool that explains selection to some extent. This is because the reason an event is likely to become news appears as the sum of its factors.

explain.alt: A news-value score table. Four events are scored from 0 to 3 on five factors: timeliness, proximity, impact, conflict, and prominence. Event A, road subsidence: 3, 3, 2, 0, 0. Event B, minister's visit: 2, 1, 1, 0, 3. Event C, festival opening: 3, 2, 1, 0, 0. Event D, budget clash: 2, 2, 3, 3, 1. There is no total column.
explain.caption: News-value score table

explain: Let us read the figure. Event D (budget clash) has the largest factor sum because its impact and conflict are high. Event A (road subsidence) is high in timeliness and proximity. Event B (minister's visit) is high only in prominence and low in the rest. Event C (festival opening) is high in timeliness but small in impact and conflict. If this score table is used as it is in an editorial meeting, the ranking can change depending on who values which factor. For example, an outlet that gives double weight to the impact factor and an outlet that gives weight to prominence produce different rankings.

Who influences selection is summarized in Shoemaker and Reese's **hierarchy of influences model**. The values and career of the **individual** reporter, **media routines** such as deadlines and article formats, **organization** such as editorial policy and ownership structure, **extra-media** forces such as advertisers, government, and sources, and **ideology**, which includes the dominant values of society, act in layers. This model emphasizes that news is produced not by one factor but by the combination of several levels.

There are limits. The score table is a tool for explaining after the fact, not a formula that determines selection. Conditions not in the table, such as a day when space is left over, series planning, and judgments of public interest, also come into play, so that events with low scores are sometimes run. In the digital environment, reader-response metrics enter editorial judgment, and readers themselves filter and spread information, so the agent of gatekeeping has become blurred. Which criteria produce good news is a normative debate, and the scores in this lesson are assumptions.

examples.title: Ranking by sum
body: Given: Rank the events in the figure's score table by the sum of their factors.
Step 1: The sums are A 3+3+2+0+0 = 8, B 2+1+1+0+3 = 7, C 3+2+1+0+0 = 6, and D 2+2+3+3+1 = 11. Step 2: The ranking is D, A, B, C.
Interpretation: If space allows 3 items, C is dropped. However, the sum adds different factors with equal weight, so changing the weights can change the ranking.

examples.title: If the weights change
body: Given: A fictional outlet that values the impact on citizens' lives gives the impact factor double weight.
Step 1: Doubling only the impact scores gives A 8 + 2 = 10, B 7 + 1 = 8, C 6 + 1 = 7, and D 11 + 3 = 14. Step 2: The ranking remains D, A, B, C.
Interpretation: This time the ranking did not change, but the gap between D and C grew from 5 to 7. The score table is a tool that lets us confirm in numbers that results can shift with the weights.

mc-11.title: The Public Sphere and Journalistic Norms: How Is Balance Calculated?
explain: What the news does does not end with conveying facts. It also serves as a forum where citizens discuss issues and form opinions. Habermas called this forum the **public sphere**, and analyzed what an ideal public sphere looks like and how it degrades in modern society.

According to Habermas, in the spaces created by the salons, coffeehouses, and early newspapers of eighteenth-century Europe, private individuals, regardless of status, debated public issues through **rational argument**. This is the bourgeois public sphere. The requirements of an ideal public sphere are summarized as openness of access, rationality of argument, and relative independence from private interests. Habermas's critique of **refeudalization** holds that as newspapers were commercialized and advertising and public relations grew, the forum of debate turned into a forum of consuming spectators. This means citizens are pushed from being the subjects of debate to being the recipients of public opinion.

There are also objections to public sphere theory. Nancy Fraser pointed out that Habermas's public sphere in practice excluded groups such as women and workers, and that the **counterpublics** these groups built separately played meaningful roles in democracy. That is, the criticism is that positing only a single ideal public sphere is the problem. This lesson is practice in reading the two positions in comparison.

The professional norms of journalism can be seen as devices for protecting the ideals of the public sphere in practice. Representative examples are **fact-checking**, **independence** from interests, the **watchdog** role of monitoring power, and **fairness and balance** on issues where opinions divide. The problem is how to implement balance. Is balance giving equal space to the positions involved, or is it reflecting the distribution of evidence and support?

**False balance** is a trap that this question produces. Consider a fictional case. On the safety of a fictional additive, Zeta-7, 95 of 100 experts hold that it is safe and 5 hold that it is dangerous. If a reporter quotes one source from each side with equal space, the reader comes to feel that opinion is split half and half. The share of the minority position among the quoted sources is 50%, while the minority share in the expert community is 5%, a difference of 45 percentage points. It looks fair on the surface but distorts the actual distribution.

That does not mean minority opinion should not be published. There are cases where a minority opinion later became the majority opinion, and minority opinion also checks the errors of the majority. One way to implement balance is to **state the distribution of support** (for example, 5 of 95 experts) and to note the level of evidence for the minority position alongside it. Not every issue is divided by evidence, either. On issues where values clash, balance of space may be more suitable. Balance is a norm whose interpretation varies with the nature of the issue.

examples.title: Reading false balance in numbers
body: Given: Forty fictional articles covered issue X, each time quoting one pro source and one con source. Of 200 experts in the field, 10 hold the opposing view.
Step 1: Since each article quoted 1 pro and 1 con, the share of con among quoted sources is 40/80 = 50%. The con share in the expert community is 10/200 = 5%.

Step 2: The difference is 50 − 5 = 45 percentage points. Interpretation: the weight of opposing opinion in the articles feels ten times larger than the real distribution. This shows the possibility of false balance. However, this figure is a standard to be used only when the issue is divided by evidence.

examples.title: Comparing public sphere critiques
body: Given: Compare the positions of Habermas and Fraser.

Step 1: Habermas sets up the ideal of a single public sphere in which rational argument is possible and criticizes its degradation through commercialization. Step 2: Fraser criticizes the exclusions of the ideal public sphere and holds that multiple counterpublics are needed.

Interpretation: The two positions are not mutually exclusive. One extends the discussion by the standard of the ideal, the other by the groups that standard missed. The learning goal is to compare them issue by issue without treating either position as the answer.

mc-12.title: Critical Media Theory: The Culture Industry, Encoding and Decoding
explain: Even when watching the same news, one person says "That's right," another says "Part of it is right, but it doesn't apply to my neighborhood," and another says "It's the exact opposite story." Should this difference be seen only as a difference in audience personality? **Critical media theory** asks about the relations among media, power, ideology, and social position.

Adorno and Horkheimer of the Frankfurt School, with the concept of the **culture industry**, criticized popular culture as standardized like factory products and as making consumers passive. In the same line, the **political economy approach** analyzes the effects of concentrated media ownership, the structure of advertising revenue, and market logic on content. These focus on the **structure** in which messages are made.

Stuart Hall of British cultural studies sees the audience as far more active. According to his **encoding/decoding model**, media producers put a **preferred meaning** into a text (encoding). Audiences, however, work out meaning according to their social position and experience (decoding). Hall distinguished three decoding positions. **Dominant-hegemonic decoding** accepts the preferred meaning as it is; **negotiated decoding** accepts the broad framework but makes exceptions for one's own circumstances; and **oppositional decoding** rejects the dominant code and reads in a different framework.

Let us read a fictional case through decoding positions. A newspaper in the fictional city of Pureun City published an article carrying the preferred meaning that "redevelopment renews the city." Reader Gap says, "Redevelopment is absolutely necessary" (dominant). Reader Eul says, "It's true that it's necessary, but it's unfair that my house is being demolished" (negotiated). Reader Byeong says, "Redevelopment is a pretext for profit and drives out residents" (oppositional). Here the decoding position is not merely for or against an opinion but the relation to how the preferred meaning was received.

When this model is used in empirical research, interviews or group discussions are classified by decoding position. If, in a fictional study, 100 Pureun City residents are classified and 38 are dominant and 22 are oppositional, the rest are negotiated, so the negotiated number is 100 − 38 − 22 = 40. Because such classification depends on the researcher's interpretation, a method is needed in which two or more people classify independently and the degree of agreement is reported (the methodology of the next stage).

Let us sort out limits and misunderstandings. Hall's model does not mean audiences make up meaning however they like. A text has a preferred meaning, and the audience's decoding is constrained by social position. Conversely, interpretations that see the audience only as passive, as in culture industry theory, often do not fit empirical research. It is good to read the two positions as a difference in how they balance structure and agency.

examples.title: Classifying statements by decoding position

mc-13.title: Network Structure and Information Diffusion
explain: While one post reaches tens of thousands of people within hours, another stops at a few friends. The difference comes not only from the quality of the content but also from **who is connected to whom**, that is, the **network structure**. Castells called a society organized around information a network society. This lesson covers the most basic tools for reading that structure.

A network consists of **nodes** (accounts) and **links** (relationships). The number of links a node has is its **degree**. How tightly knit the whole network is is measured by its **density**. When there are $n$ nodes, the number of possible links is $n(n-1)/2$, and if there are $L$ actual links, the density $d$ is $L$ divided by the number of possible links. $$d = \frac{L}{n(n-1)/2}$$ The distance between nodes is measured as the minimum number of links passed through to go from one node to another.

explain.alt: A network drawing 7 accounts as circles and follow relationships as lines. The three accounts A, B, and C form a triangle, all connected to each other. A connects to D, and D connects to E. E connects to F and to G. There are 7 lines in total.
explain.caption: A small social network

explain: The figure is a fictional network of 7 accounts. A, B, and C form a triangle all connected to each other, and A-D, D-E, E-F, and E-G are the remaining links. There are 7 links, and the number of possible links is $7 \times 6 / 2 = 21$, so the density is $7/21 = 1/3$. The degree is largest, 3, for A and E. To go from A to F, one must pass through three links, A-D, D-E, and E-F, so the distance is 3. Along this path, D and E act as a **bridge** connecting one cluster to another.

The sociologist Granovetter argued that **weak ties** connecting different clusters often bring new information more than the **strong ties** among close friends. Close friends share the same information, but weak ties carry information from other clusters. In the figure, if the A-D link is cut, {A, B, C} and {D, E, F, G} split into two. Such a link is the channel through which information crosses between the two clusters.

Diffusion can be approximated with a simple model. Suppose a person who sees a post exposes it to an average of $k$ people, and shares it with probability $p$ among them. The average number of additional shares produced by one share is $R = k \times p$. For example, if $k = 8$ and $p = 0.15$, then $R = 1.2$. If $R$ is greater than 1, diffusion continues on average, and if it is less than 1, it eventually fades out. This is a simplification borrowing the idea of epidemic spread models.

There are limits. This model assumes all nodes have the same $k$ and $p$, but in reality a small number of accounts with very many followers (hubs) govern diffusion. Also, if the same person sees the same post by several routes, they are exposed after having already seen it, so actual new reach shrinks. Therefore $R$ is a scale for gauging the possibility of diffusion, not a predicted value.

Step 1: Starting from B, cross to A. Step 2: Passing A-D, D-E, and E-G in turn gives four links, B-A-D-E-G. The distance is 4.
Interpretation: On this path, A-D and D-E are the only channels. If these links are cut, G cannot be reached from {B}. Accounts that serve as bridges have a large influence on information diffusion.

Interpretation: At R = 1, spread is sustained on average, and at 1.5, diffusion tends to continue. Even for the same content, a small change in sharing probability greatly changes the pattern of diffusion. However, diffusion does not mean accuracy or value.

mc-14.title: Platform Algorithms and the Filter Bubble Debate
explain: When you turn on your smartphone, a feed appears as if someone had set its order. Which posts rise to the top and which are buried is decided by a **recommendation algorithm**. This algorithm performs gatekeeping in a different way from a newspaper editor-in-chief. It produces countless personalized lists based not on a person but on data about the user's past behavior.

The basic structure is this. For each candidate post, it **predicts** values such as the probability the user will click, the time they will spend viewing, and the probability they will react; combines these values into a **score**; and then shows posts in descending order of score. Collaborative filtering is a method of predicting from "what people who behaved similarly to me liked." What the platform puts into the score and how much weight it gives becomes, in effect, its editorial policy.

explain.alt: A table of predicted values for 5 candidate posts. 1 Friend update: predicted click probability 40%, predicted dwell 20 seconds. 2 Controversial video: 60%, 50 seconds. 3 Local notice: 20%, 10 seconds. 4 Hobby clip: 50%, 30 seconds. 5 New-topic article: 30%, 40 seconds. Below it is written "score = 0.5 × click probability + 0.5 × dwell time."
explain.caption: Predicted values for candidate posts

explain: The score in the figure is computed as $0.5 \times$ click probability $+ 0.5 \times$ dwell time. Post 2 is $0.5 \times 60 + 0.5 \times 50 = 55$, post 4 is $0.5 \times 50 + 0.5 \times 30 = 40$, post 5 is $0.5 \times 30 + 0.5 \times 40 = 35$, post 1 is $0.5 \times 40 + 0.5 \times 20 = 30$, and post 3 is $0.5 \times 20 + 0.5 \times 10 = 15$. So the ranking is 2, 4, 5, 1, 3. If the weights change, the ranking changes too. Giving 0.8 to click probability and 0.2 to dwell makes post 2 58, post 4 46, post 1 36, and post 5 32, so post 1 comes ahead of post 5. What to put into the score is both a technical matter and a matter of values.

The concern that algorithms narrow the information users see is the **filter bubble**. Pariser popularized the term in 2011. An **echo chamber** is the phenomenon in which, in a space where only similar opinions circulate, the same opinion reverberates and conviction grows; Sunstein and others discussed it. The two concepts are distinct. The filter bubble is a problem of what the algorithm filters out, while the echo chamber also includes users' own choices to gather with similar people and the problem of social interaction.

There is a way to measure diversity of exposure with numbers. If the share of the i-th source in a feed is $s_i$, using $H = \sum s_i^2$ as the **Herfindahl index** gives a value near 1 when concentrated in one place and smaller when spread evenly. If three sources have shares of 50%, 30%, and 20%, then $H = 0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.38$. If three sources had equal shares, $3 \times (1/3)^2 = 0.333$, so 0.38 is somewhat concentrated. However, this index looks at only one aspect of diversity (skew in sources).

The evidence in this debate is mixed. Some studies report that algorithmic recommendation narrows users' information environment, while others report that most users are exposed to more diverse sources than expected and that individual choice plays a larger role. It is hard to separate the algorithm from individual choice, and it differs by platform. So rather than asserting, one needs the attitude of checking which evidence came from which conditions. Transparency and whether users can adjust the recommendation method are separate issues.

Interpretation: 0.58 shows more concentration than 0.50. However, whether the difference between the two values is a meaningful concentration in practice, and whether its cause is the algorithm or the user's choices, cannot be known from these numbers alone.

mc-15.title: Media Ecology: How Do Media Change Society?
explain: A person who wrote letters and a person who uses a messenger app speak differently even when they say the same thing. Writing, print, the telegraph, broadcasting, and the internet have changed not only the content conveyed but also the way people think and form relationships. **Media ecology** views media as an environment and asks how that environment shapes people and society.

Innis held that media biased toward time (durable media such as stone) and media biased toward space (light media that travel far, such as paper) organize societies differently. Ong discussed how oral culture and literate culture make modes of thought different. McLuhan, with the phrase "the medium is the message," emphasized the changes made by the medium itself rather than by its content. Postman carried this on into changes in education and political discourse.

McLuhan and his son Eric summarized four questions for analyzing a medium as the **laws of media (tetrad)**. What does this medium **enhance**? What does this medium **obsolesce**? What from the past does this medium **retrieve**? And when pushed to the extreme, what does it **reverse** into? It is a framework that has four questions read a single medium in three dimensions.

Let us apply it to a fictional case. A fictional medium, the "voice memo app," has become widespread. What it enhances is the immediacy of speech and the conveying of emotion. What it obsolesces is the habit of organizing thoughts in writing and sending them. What it retrieves is speaking and listening of oral culture. Its reversal is that memos pile up so much that they become unlistened-to noise. Since this is a framework of questions rather than a problem with a fixed answer, it is important to argue while giving grounds.

The speed at which media spread is explained by Rogers's **diffusion of innovations theory**. Adopters of a new technology are divided in time order into **innovators** (about 2.5%), **early adopters** (about 13.5%), **early majority** (about 34%), **late majority** (about 34%), and **laggards** (about 16%). Cumulative adoption traces an S-shaped curve. When a new service spreads among 2,000 residents of a village, innovators and early adopters together are about 16%, so about 320 people use it first.

There are limits. **Technological determinism**, the view that media determine society, collides with the reality that the same medium is used differently in different societies. The fact that the same printing technology produced different results in Europe and East Asia is discussed as a common counterexample. It should be read together with the objection of **social constructionism**, which holds that society chooses media and decides their uses. The four laws are only a tool for generating hypotheses, not a tool for proving them.

body: Given: Analyze a fictional medium, a "short video summary service," with the four laws.

Step 1: Enhancement is the ability to grasp only the essentials quickly, and obsolescence is the habit of reading a long text to the end. Step 2: Retrieval is the short stories passed on by word of mouth, and reversal is fragments of information whose context has vanished because they were cut down too far.
Interpretation: All four are hypotheses. Whether they are actually so must be checked through surveys of usage behavior and comparative research.

Step 1: Those who use it first are 5,000 × 0.16 = 800. Step 2: The cumulative figure including the early majority is 2.5 + 13.5 + 34 = 50%, which is 2,500.
Interpretation: The point at which half use it is near the inflection point of the S-curve. Rogers's proportions are a typical distribution, and not every technology follows them.

mc-16.title: Content Analysis and Intercoder Reliability
explain: To say "This newspaper reports a lot of conflict" is only an impression. To turn it into research, you must read the articles and **count by the same criteria**. **Content analysis** is a method of systematically and objectively classifying and quantifying the characteristics of media texts. This lesson centers on the step of checking whether the classification can be trusted.

The procedure is roughly this. Set the research question and draw a **sample** from the set of articles to be analyzed. Decide the **unit of analysis** (one article, a paragraph, a sentence, and so on) that determines what is counted as one, and define the **categories** for classification. The document that records the definitions and examples of the categories is the **codebook**. Train the coders, run a pilot coding on part of the material, and once it passes the **reliability check**, code everything and analyze. Of these, reliability is the center of this lesson.

Reliability is the degree to which two or more people, classifying independently with the same codebook, produce the same results. The simplest measure is **percent agreement**, the proportion that the two coders classified the same way. But percent agreement includes the share that matched by chance. Even if two people classify as if flipping a coin, about half will agree. So we use a measure that subtracts chance agreement, **Cohen's kappa**.

Kappa compares the observed agreement with the agreement expected by chance. $$\kappa = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e}$$ $P_o$는 관찰된 일치율, $P_e$ (P_o is the observed agreement; P_e is the agreement expected by chance from the two coders' classification proportions). Chance agreement is found by summing, over the categories, the product of the proportions in which the two coders assigned that category.

explain.alt: A cross-tabulation of two coders' classifications (100 articles, is a conflict frame present). The cell where coder A says present and coder B also says present is 30, A present and B absent is 10, row total 40. A absent and B present is 5, both absent is 55, row total 60. The column totals are B present 35, B absent 65, overall 100.
explain.caption: The two coders' classification results

explain: Let us read the cross-tabulation in the figure. There are 30 articles that both coders saw as present and 55 that both saw as absent, so $P_o = (30 + 55)/100 = 0.85$. The proportion coder A classified as present is 0.40 and for coder B it is 0.35, so the chance expectation for both present is $0.40 \times 0.35 = 0.14$, and for both absent is $0.60 \times 0.65 = 0.39$. $P_e = 0.14 + 0.39 = 0.53$, and $\kappa = (0.85 - 0.53)/(1 - 0.53) = 0.32/0.47 \approx 0.68$. Percent agreement is high at 85%, but the agreement with chance removed is 0.68. The standard for how much is enough is just convention (such as calling 0.6 to 0.8 substantial agreement) and varies with field and purpose.

You should also know the limits. When one category is very frequent, there is a phenomenon where percent agreement is high but kappa comes out low. Also, a high kappa does not mean the category definitions are valid. Two coders can be wrong in the same way. Reliability is a necessary condition for validity, not a sufficient one. That is why the codebook is made public and the results of the checks and the revision process are reported together.

mc-17.title: Experimental Design: Testing the Causal Effect of Frames
explain: Content analysis and surveys can show an **association** such as "people exposed to a certain frame oppose more." But those people may have been inclined to oppose to begin with and so sought out news with that frame. To confirm whether the frame **changed** attitudes, an **experiment**, in which the researcher decides the exposure, is needed.

The basic structure of an experiment is this. Participants are divided into groups **at random** (random assignment). One group is shown an article with Frame A, another group an article with Frame B, and yet another group (the **control group**) a neutral article. Then attitudes are measured with the same questions. Thanks to random assignment, the groups can be regarded as similar from the start on average, so differences between groups can be interpreted as the effect of the treatment. This advantage is the core of the experiment.

explain.alt: A bar chart of the average attitude scores of three groups. The control group is 4.0, the Frame A group is 5.0, and the Frame B group is 3.5. The vertical axis is average attitude on a scale of 1 to 7, and it is noted that 50 people per group were randomly assigned.
explain.caption: Average attitude scores of three groups

explain: The figure is a fictional result in which 50 people per group were asked about their attitudes on a scale of 1 to 7. The control group average is 4.0, the Frame A group 5.0, and the Frame B group 3.5. The effect is the treatment group average minus the control group average, so Frame A is +1.0 and Frame B is −0.5. Whether this difference is large or small must be compared against the spread of the scores (the standard deviation). The difference divided by the standard deviation is the **effect size** (Cohen's $d$). In the formula below, $T$ is the treatment group and $C$ is the control group. $$d = \frac{\bar{x}_T - \bar{x}_C}{s}$$ 표준편차 $s$가 2.0이라면 프레임 가는 $d = 1.0/2.0 = 0.5$, 프레임 나는 $d = -0.5/2.0 = -0.25$이다. (In English: if the standard deviation s is 2.0, Frame A has d = 0.5 and Frame B has d = -0.25.)

The benchmarks for large and small effect sizes (the convention that 0.2 is small, 0.5 is medium, and 0.8 is large) differ by field. The same $d$ can mean different things in real society. Also, a difference in means can appear by chance, so a **statistical significance** test or a confidence interval is reported alongside. This lesson covers it only at the conceptual level.

There are several items commonly checked in design. A **manipulation check** is a question asking whether the frame was perceived as intended. A **confounding variable** is a factor that varies along with the treatment and contaminates the result; for example, if one group's text is longer, length becomes a confound. **Internal validity** is the degree to which the causal interpretation is correct, and **external validity** is the degree to which the result generalizes to reality outside the experiment.

The limits are clear. In the laboratory, participants are forced to read a single article, but in reality they choose what to read and are exposed to multiple frames. If the sample is skewed toward university students, generalization is difficult. Also, how long the effect of a single exposure lasts is hard to know from one experiment. So experiments are read together with surveys that use real-world data. Designs that deceive participants require debriefing and ethics review.

examples.title: Effect and effect size
body: Given: The three group means in the figure (4.0, 5.0, 3.5) and a standard deviation of 2.0.
Step 1: The effect of Frame A is 5.0 − 4.0 = 1.0, d = 1.0/2.0 = 0.5. Step 2: The effect of Frame B is 3.5 − 4.0 = −0.5, d = −0.25.

Interpretation: Frame A raises attitudes and Frame B lowers them. The directions are opposite and the size of A is twice that of B. Speaking only of size and leaving out the sign loses the information about direction.

examples.title: Finding design flaws
body: Given: A fictional researcher had students in a morning class read the Frame A article and students in an afternoon class read the Frame B article.

Step 1: Because the two groups are not random, differences between morning and afternoon students (major, fatigue, disposition) become confounding variables. Step 2: Even if an attitude difference arises, it cannot be separated whether it is due to the frame or to the class time slot.
Interpretation: Randomly dividing students of the same class into two groups and having them read at the same time can reduce this confound.

mc-18.title: Survey Design: Sampling, Error, and Items
explain: Opinion polls appear often in the news, but without knowing the design hidden behind the numbers, they are easy to misread. What does the sentence "1,000 respondents, margin of error ±3.1 percentage points" mean? The credibility of a **survey** depends on who was selected and how (**sampling**), how large the error arising from a small sample is (**sampling error**), and how the questions were written (**items**).

The principle of sampling is that the probability of each member of the population being selected must be known. In **simple random sampling**, everyone is selected with equal probability, and in **stratified sampling**, the population is divided into strata such as region or age and samples are drawn from each stratum. In contrast, a voluntary vote on an internet portal is a **self-selected** sample. Even if 8,000 people take part, the people who would take part were separately determined, so it is hard to say it represents the population. How the sample is gathered matters more than how many are gathered.

When estimating a proportion in random sampling, the sampling error (margin of error) $e$ is approximately as follows. $$e = z \times \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$$ $n$은 표본 크기, $p$는 비율, $z$는 신뢰수준 95%에서 약 1.96이다. 가장 보수적인 경우 $p = 0.5$를 쓴다. $n = 400$이면 $\sqrt{0.25/400} = 0.025$이고 오차범위는 $1.96 \times 0.025 = 0.049$, i.e., ±4.9 percentage points. (In English: n is the sample size, p is the proportion, and z is about 1.96 at a 95% confidence level; in the most conservative case use p = 0.5. For n = 400, the square root term is 0.025.)

One can also work backward to find the sample size. If you want a margin of error $e$, then $n = z^2 \times p(1-p)/e^2$. If you want ±5 percentage points, $n = (1.96/0.05)^2 \times 0.25 = 1536.64 \times 0.25 = 384.16$, which is rounded up to 385 people. If you want ±3 percentage points, about 1,068 people are needed. To cut the error in half, the sample must be quadrupled. This relationship regarding sample size is why large samples are expensive.

The margin of error speaks only of chance variation in **random sampling**. The bias of people who did not respond (**nonresponse bias**), the influence of question wording, and the problem of people left out of the sampling frame (such as a phone directory) are not included in the margin of error. That is why this formula cannot be used for self-selected samples.

There are common flaws in item design. A **leading question** uses wording that nudges toward a particular response. A **double-barreled question** asks two different things in one item. If **response categories** overlap or leave gaps, classification becomes unstable. A **Likert scale** measures attitude in steps from strongly disagree to strongly agree, and the number of steps and the presence of a middle option affect responses. Items are checked with a pilot survey, and measuring the same concept with several items allows checking reliability.

examples.title: Calculating the margin of error
body: Given: Random sampling with n = 900, p = 0.5 because the proportion is unknown, and a 95% confidence level.
Step 1: $\sqrt{0.25/900} = 0.5/30 = 0.01667$. Step 2: The margin of error is $1.96 \times 0.01667 = 0.0327$, that is, about ±3.3 percentage points.

Interpretation: If the support rate for one item comes out at 48%, the population value is read as roughly between 44.7% and 51.3%. The error for the difference between the support rates of two items is larger than this and must be calculated separately.

examples.title: Fixing an item
body: Given: The fictional item is "Do you agree with the opinion that the government's wasteful broadcasting subsidies should be ended?"

Step 1: It contains the value-judgment word "wasteful," so it is a leading question. Step 2: Change it to a neutral "What do you think about the government's broadcasting subsidy program?" and give non-overlapping options such as continue, reduce, and end.
Interpretation: Even for the same issue, support rates can differ with question wording, so the wording should be made public.

checks.explanation: Rounding 384.16 up gives 385. To cut the error in half (±2.5 percentage points) requires about 4 times as many.

checks.explanation: Even a large sample is not accurate if it is biased. Representativeness comes from the method of selection.

The two surveys have the same reliability
Random sampling is useless because the responses are few

checks.explanation: A respondent who is satisfied with the speed but dissatisfied with the design cannot answer. It should be asked as two separate items.
options: How many times did you see the news during the past week?
How often do you use this app?
Would you be willing to recommend this app to an acquaintance?
Are you satisfied with the speed and design of this app?

mc-19.title: Integrated Problem-Solving: A Local News Research Case
explain: So far we have learned effects theory, journalism, networks and algorithms, and research methods separately. Real research uses these tools together on a single problem. This lesson practices cross-cutting reasoning through a research case about the local newspaper Saebyeok Daily in the fictional city of Saebyeok City.

Situation: A research team wants to know the relationship between "how much Saebyeok Daily covers the transportation issue" and "whether citizens name transportation as the most important problem." The first step is to connect the research question to theory. This is a question of first-level agenda-setting. The two variables must be measured separately, with a time lag. Without knowing the theory, one cannot know what to measure.

The second step is measurement. To run a content analysis of newspaper articles, a codebook and two coders are needed. Suppose the coders independently classified 100 articles as "is it a transportation issue article," with 45 seen as yes by both, 5 seen as yes by coder A only, 15 seen as yes by coder B only, and 35 seen as no by both. $P_o = 0.80$. A's yes proportion is 0.50 and B's is 0.60, so $P_e = 0.50 \times 0.60 + 0.50 \times 0.40 = 0.50$ and $\kappa = (0.80 - 0.50)/(1 - 0.50) = 0.60$. Although percent agreement is high, with chance agreement removed it is 0.60, so it is better to refine the codebook further.

The third step is the survey. Draw a random sample of 1,000 citizens and ask them about the "most important problem." When estimating a proportion, the maximum margin of error is $1.96 \times \sqrt{0.25/1000} \approx 0.031$, that is, about ±3.1 percentage points. A result that 36% named transportation is read as roughly between 33% and 39%. This does not include the bias of people who did not respond or wording effects.

The fourth step is interpretation. Even if the rankings of coverage share and citizen responses match, we cannot assert agenda-setting. The newspaper may have followed citizens' interests (the reverse direction), or the same event may have influenced both. Moreover, if citizens get information from social media recommendation feeds, the influence of newspaper coverage may be small, and the feed's algorithm may be what produces the issue ranking. Designing a study that lists such alternative explanations and checks each one is integrated problem-solving.

The fifth step is an honest statement of limits. Data from one newspaper in one city at one point in time cannot be generalized. The researcher must write separately which conclusions come directly from the data and which are conjecture. The items in this lesson follow this flow and ask in turn about theory, measurement, statistics, and interpretation.

examples.title: Mapping theory to research evidence
body: Given: The Saebyeok City research team sets up four hypotheses. (A) Coverage volume transfers citizens' issue rankings. (B) The worldview of those who have watched for a long time comes to resemble broadcasting. (C) People who feel they are in the minority reduce expressing their opinions. (D) Editors have criteria for selecting articles.

Step 1: (A) is a comparison of time-lagged coverage volume and responses; (B) is a comparison of the difference in perceptions between heavy and light viewers; (C) is a comparison of willingness to express opinion publicly by opinion; and (D) is the ratio of incoming to published articles together with observation of editorial meetings.
Step 2: Knowing what data each theory requires makes the research realistic. Interpretation: A theory is tested only when it is translated into a measurable form.

examples.title: Sample size and error
body: Given: What happens to the margin of error if the Saebyeok City survey is reduced from n = 1,000 to n = 250?
Step 1: With n = 1,000 the margin of error is about 3.1 percentage points. Step 2: With n = 250, $\sqrt{0.25/250} = 0.0316$ and $1.96 \times 0.0316 = 0.0620$, about 6.2 percentage points.
Interpretation: Cutting the sample to a quarter doubles the margin of error. When cutting the budget, we can explain in numbers how accuracy changes.

checks.prompt: Arrange the flow of the Saebyeok City study in order.
checks.hint: Theory, then measurement tools, then data collection, then interpretation.
checks.explanation: The reliability check is done before coding everything, and interpretation and the statement of limits come last.

Create a codebook and check intercoder reliability
Code newspaper articles and administer the citizen survey
Interpret the results and write the alternative explanations and limits

checks.explanation: Time order reduces the possibility of the reverse direction but does not remove third factors.

mc-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Designing a Study of the Effect of Media Frames on Public Opinion
explain: This lesson is a design task, not an assessment. In a fictional case, you design a study that tests "the effect of media frames on citizens' policy support." Since it is not a problem with a right answer, the evaluation criterion is explaining your choices on the basis of the theories and methods learned earlier.

Fictional case: Saebyeok City plans to introduce a "private-car restriction zone downtown." Some Saebyeok Daily articles put "improving air quality" first, and others put "merchants' loss of sales" first. The research question is "Do these two frames have different effects on citizens' policy support?" First choose the theory. Framing (emphasis framing), priming (activation of evaluation criteria), the spiral of silence (expression of minority opinion), and decoding positions (the audience's position) are candidates.

Next is the choice of method. For a question asking about causal effect, a **randomized experiment** is suitable. There are three groups, an air-quality frame, a sales frame, and a neutral (control) group, and the dependent variable is policy support (1 to 7 points). Include manipulation-check items and control of confounding variables (such as article length and displayed author names) in the design. Conversely, if you want to know "which frames Saebyeok Daily actually uses more," **content analysis** is right, and then a codebook and intercoder reliability are needed. "The level of support among all citizens" is measured by a random-sample **survey**, calculating the sample size and margin of error.

There are questions for checking each element of the design. Who is in the sample and how is it gathered? How many people per group, and at what effect size will the result be considered meaningful? How are variables measured? How are results reported (mean difference, effect size, confidence interval)? What alternative explanations are expected? How will research ethics be observed (voluntary participation, privacy protection, debriefing)?

Ethics and limits are also part of the design. The articles shown to participants in an experiment require that the research purpose be explained afterward, and content that slanders real existing institutions or people must not be used. The design document should state that there are limits to generalizing laboratory results to reality, that the data cover one issue and one city, and that the persistence of the effect cannot be known.

The items below check the earlier concepts once, have you write the research question in one sentence using a keyword-style response, and then lead you to write a design document as a submitted task. The submitted task has no score and is something you improve yourself with the checklist, and your text is saved only on this device.

examples.title: A model design outline
body: Given: A frame-effect experiment on the Saebyeok City private-car restriction zone.

Step 1: Randomly assign 300 citizens to three groups (air-quality frame, sales frame, neutral), 100 each, and have them read fictional articles of the same length. Step 2: Measure policy support (1 to 7 points) and manipulation-check items, and compare mean differences and effect sizes.
Interpretation: Random assignment and the neutral control make a causal interpretation possible. Because real-world selective exposure cannot be handled, it is supplemented by a follow-up survey.

examples.title: A mixed design outline
body: Given: Check the same problem with real-world data.

Step 1: Run a content analysis of three months of Saebyeok Daily articles to obtain the share of frames (two coders, kappa reported). Step 2: Measure policy support with a survey of 1,000 citizens (margin of error ±3.1 percentage points) and make a time-lagged comparison.

Interpretation: The causal interpretation of the experiment and the ecological validity of real-world data complement each other. However, state the limit that the interpretation remains at the level of association.

checks.explanation: The nature of the question determines the method.

checks.explanation: This item does not pass automatically. Compare with the model answer and check the checklist items one by one.
checks.model: The research question is "Do the air-quality improvement frame and the sales-loss frame have different effects on citizens' support for the private-car restriction policy?" The independent variable is the frame of the article citizens read (air quality, sales, neutral), and the dependent variable is the policy support score (1 to 7 points). It is an experiment in which 300 citizens are randomly assigned to three groups, and mean differences and effect sizes are compared. It includes a manipulation check and control of article length, and states that there are limits to generalizing laboratory results.
